description: Next to the University of Newcastle, this project maximises a constrained site by retaining a 4-bedroom dwelling and adding a 7-bedroom boarding house. Complex planning constraints were resolved with highly efficient design, leaving just 2sqm unused. The result is a low-maintenance, energy-efficient student living asset.
long_description:
Adjacent to the University of Newcastle, this project delivers a compact, high-performing student boarding house on an exceptionally constrained site. Despite the lot being below the minimum subdivision size, the brief was to maximise yield while maintaining functionality and amenity. Benchmarking against a neighbouring property that achieved a single 7-bedroom boarding house, the design successfully retained the existing 4-bedroom dwelling while introducing an additional 7-bedroom boarding house—significantly increasing the site’s capacity.
The site was heavily constrained by planning envelope controls, a large rear power easement, and a main sewer line running through the buildable area, making spatial efficiency critical. The design resolves these limitations through precise planning, leaving only 2sqm of unutilised site area. Operational efficiency was a key driver, with integrated systems such as keyed power controls to manage energy use, alongside a passively designed building envelope with carefully modelled eaves for seasonal performance. The roof was oriented for a future 10kW solar array, later installed.
Andrew led the design and administered the construction contract, delivering a highly efficient, low-maintenance asset that performs environmentally and operationally for student living.
title: Student Accommodation

description: Originally constructed between 1910 and 1925, when Bridge Street was the terminus of one of Newcastle’s tram routes, this home had undergone several unsympathetic additions that obscured its original character. Combined with extensive termite damage and significant foundation failure, the building had deteriorated to the point where demolition was a genuine consideration. The brief was to restore the home's historic character while replacing the fragmented series of skillion additions with a cohesive and contemporary family living environment.
long_description:
Originally constructed between 1910 and 1925, when Bridge Street was the terminus of one of Newcastle’s tram routes, this home had undergone several unsympathetic additions that obscured its original character. Combined with extensive termite damage and significant foundation failure, the building had deteriorated to the point where demolition was a genuine consideration. The brief was to restore the home's historic character while replacing the fragmented series of skillion additions with a cohesive and contemporary family living environment.
The design reinstates key heritage elements, including the bullnose verandah and traditional detailing, while introducing a carefully integrated rear extension beneath a unified roof form. A generous open-plan living, dining, and kitchen space opens to the north-east, capturing morning sunlight and connecting to a deep outdoor entertaining area overlooking the pool. The project also became a testing ground for smart home technology, including an automated floor heating system that activates only when surplus solar energy is being generated, allowing the home to store renewable energy as thermal mass. The completed project transforms a failing structure into a light-filled four-bedroom home with a self-contained secondary dwelling, combining heritage restoration, contemporary living, and sustainable performance in a single cohesive design.
title: Bridge St Heritage Extension

description: Extension of a circa 1900 Federation dairy house in Maitland, adding a generous master suite, new living areas, and a converted studio outbuilding. A hillside wine and root vegetable store and reworked porte-cochère driveway complete the cohesive rural site masterplan.
long_description:
Located in Maitland NSW, this extension of the original Cleveland Dairy house needed to work seamlessly with the existing house. The existing Federation dwelling, a circa 1900 dairy house with its surrounding sheds operated as a hobby farm, with the client seeking to expand the home to include a generous master suite and new living areas that sit comfortably within the character of the original building. In a second project the brief evolved to incorporate the conversion of an existing outbuilding into a self-contained studio with bathroom and kitchenette, extending the functionality of the site.

The design adopts a sympathetic approach, introducing a simple-form extension that aligns with the proportions and material language of the existing house. A broader masterplan coordinates site access, including a reworked driveway with porte-cochère providing a formal sheltered entry, and provision for a future secondary dwelling.

A wine and root vegetable store responds to the client's interest in food and wine and was embedded into the hillside beneath the house. The store, which opened onto a tasting court, combines thermal performance with framed views toward Maitland. Natural stone, earthworks, and battered grassed forms are used to integrate the intervention into the landscape, balancing cut and fill to create a grounded and cohesive outcome.
title: The Old Dairy House

description: This project is the redevelopment of a constrained corner site in urban Adamstown, located within walking distance of Adamstown Station, into a compact multi-unit housing scheme.
long_description:
The 2 new buildings are conceived as new generation boarding houses each containing 4 Micro-apartments. The site design retains the existing dwelling for refurbishment which both increased project viability allowing it to be sold to fund the construction whilst retaining the materials of the house after renovation to reduce construction waste sent to landfill.
Working within tight envelope controls and a narrow site geometry, the primary challenge was to maximise development yield while maintaining liveability and a coherent streetscape response for long-term ownership and management by the client.
The design was developed from first principles, testing buildable volumes against solar access, cross-ventilation, and spatial efficiency to ensure each apartment benefits from strong environmental performance. 
A strong sustainability agenda informed every stage of the project, including building orientation, integrated solar shading, roof forms designed for maximised photovoltaic potential, low-VOC material selections, and water capture and reuse strategies. 
Bicycle storage and reduced reliance on private vehicles were prioritised in response to the clients aims and was enabled by the site’s proximity to public transport, reinforcing a low-carbon lifestyle model. The resulting development delivers efficient, well-resolved housing that balances yield, environmental performance, and long-term operational intent.
title: Adamstown Multi-Unit

description: Located in Lorn, this project complements the restoration of a 1920s Californian bungalow with a new garage and covered patio designed to feel as though they had always belonged to the property. The brief called for a sympathetic addition that respected the character of the original home while enhancing its connection to the garden. Rather than competing with the heritage building, the new work draws on the homes original architectural language to create a cohesive and timeless outcome.
long_description:
Located in Lorn, this project complements the restoration of a 1920s Californian bungalow with a new garage and covered patio designed to feel as though they had always belonged to the property. The brief called for a sympathetic addition that respected the character of the original home while enhancing its connection to the garden. Rather than competing with the heritage building, the new work draws on the homes original architectural language to create a cohesive and timeless outcome.
The garage echoes the proportions and detailing of the original bugalow, incorporating matching brickwork and panelling, roof form, and a prominent Dutch gable to reinforce the relationship between old and new. A covered patio extends seamlessly from the raised deck, creating a step-free connection between the house, outdoor living area, driveway, and garage. Designed to become enveloped by climbing plants over time, the structure softens the transition between the home and its landscape. 
Andrew Barnard led the design and planning approval process, providing ongoing advice during construction and post-completion guidance on privacy and site integration. The completed restoration, including these additions, was recognised with the 2024 Master Builders Association Award for Heritage Restoration, celebrating the quality and sensitivity of the overall project.
title: Garage and Patio

description: The owners of this cottage in Hamilton approached Andrew to design a sympathetic extension of their heritage listed home in Hamilton, Newcastle.
long_description:
The client wanted to create a larger and more cohesive living, dining and kitchen area which could open onto the rear courtyard. The design also included a large double study and library for the client home office. 
The proposed design incorporates a single garage which blends into the dwelling. The owners also wanted an undercover area at the front entry so a port-cochere was introduced providing undercover arrival and unloading of groceries and family.
title: Hamilton Heritage Extension

description: Set on a rural property in Bolwarra, this project involved the staged expansion of an existing prefabricated home, including a third-bedroom extension, new pool, double stacked garage with workshop and gym, and a basketball court. The site, a rural home to an equestrian family, presented significant constraints due to extensive flood-prone areas, technically bushfire constrained requiring careful positioning of all new works within a limited buildable footprint and detailed justification to Council for the BAL level proposed. The design response balanced these constraints with the client’s brief for a cohesive rural lifestyle upgrade.
long_description:
The architectural approach maintained continuity with the existing dwelling’s external materials and character, while introducing a more refined and contemporary internal language. Multiple iterations of design were developed for the garage to optimise function, access, and integration with the broader site layout. 
A key feature of the project was the seamless incorporation of a “shipping container pool” system, coordinated alongside consultants and engineering inputs. The project required considerable negotiation with Council, ensuring compliance within the flood-affected zoning context. The result is a highly functional rural estate that enhances amenity, supports an active family lifestyle, and sits comfortably within its landscape setting.
title: Rural Extension and Garage

description: Crest Financial Offices is the adaptive reuse of a former Salvation Army hall in East Maitland. Reimagined as a contemporary “home branch” for the growing financial services team.
long_description:
The design responds to a series of complex constraints, including fire rating requirements driven by boundary proximity, a fragmented existing floor level, and a significant level change of approximately 1.2 metres above the street. A key challenge was overcoming the building’s setback, which created a disconnect from High Street, while establishing a clear and welcoming presence for clients.
The proposal introduces a new entry awning that acts as a visual marker from the street, drawing visitors into the building and anchoring a reconfigured internal layout of private offices and open-plan workspaces for up to 30 staff. Accessibility is resolved through a carefully integrated sequence of level transitions, avoiding reliance on mechanical lifts while maintaining equitable access throughout. A client-focused reception space incorporates a coffee hub, reinforcing a more informal and hospitable experience. The resulting workplace is a light-filled, highly functional environment that supports the daily operations of financial advisors and accounts staff, while reconnecting the building to the rhythm and fabric of High Street.

Project team:
Architect: Andrew Barnard
Builder: NJG Construction
Disability Access Consultant: Lindsay Perry
Hydraulic Fire: Marline
Quantity Surveyor: Muller Partnership
Land Survey: Rennie Golledge
Traffic Engineer: Intersect Traffic
title: Crest Financial Office
